newsitem.title: USA: Committees let states contract out welfare programs.
newsitem.headline: Committees let states contract out welfare programs.

text.p: House committees voted Thursday to let states hire private firms to administer their food stamp and Medicaid programmes for the poor, overturning White House policy.

As part of legislation to implement a five-year balanced budget deal, the House Agriculture and Commerce Committees voted to expand state authority to contract out what has been a government function.

Texas officials want to hire a private company to run many of their social programmes in an effort to cut costs and consolidate services as they reform their welfare system. The White House rejected much of the state's request.
The Commerce Committee voted 27-20 to let states bring companies on board to determine eligibility for Medicaid benefits.

The agriculture panel voted 24-19 to allow private firms to administer part of the food stamp programme. The provision was part of a larger bill allocating $1.5 billion for job training for Food Stamp recipients and exempting some able-bodied individuals from tough new limits on aid.
Many Democrats on the Commerce Committee voted against the Medicaid proposal, calling it a major change in the programme that provides health care for poor, elderly and disabled Americans.

"Private companies are accountable to their shareholders ... not the taxpayers. I have some concern about someone making a determination for eligibility who may be getting a (financial) benefit for disqualifying" prople, said Gene Green, a Texas Democrat.

Wisconsin Republican Scott Klug argued that his state could save at least 20 percent of programme costs by using a more efficient private firm. States and the federal government would still set programme rules.
Food stamps are the major U.S. antihunger programme, helping more than 20 million poor people a month buy groceries.

Representative Larry Combest, Texas Republican and author of the amendment, said his state could save millions if it could hire private contractors to determine if applicants were eligible for food stamps.
"We have had absolute, total opposition to do anything" from the White House, said Representative Charles Stenholm, Texas Democrat, in explaining why congressional action was sought.

Only one Democrat joined Stenholm in voting for the proposal while Republicans uniformly backed it. Most Democrats called the Texas proposal untested and unlikely to actually save any money but certain to displace government workers.
Two of the top-ranking Republicans in the House, Texans Dick Armey and Tom DeLay, signed a letter asking colleagues to support the plan.

The legislation will be wrapped into a so-called budget reconciliation bill to carry out terms of the balanced budget pact passed by Congress. The Senate Agriculture Committee approved the additional $1.5 billion earlier this week.

During its session, the House Agriculture Committee rejected, 30-13, a Stenholm amemdnent to cap the amount of money given to states for running the food stamp programme. The White House, governors and legislators opposed it.
